Otolaryngology · published research

Palatal myoclonus

Two case reports described marked reductions in palatal tremor frequency, with reported improvement in swallowing or sleep. The uncontrolled observations cannot distinguish a treatment effect from natural variation or other influences.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Two case reports described marked reductions in palatal tremor frequency, with reported improvement in swallowing or sleep. The uncontrolled observations cannot distinguish a treatment effect from natural variation or other influences.

Summary of the Evidence

The category contains one publication describing two cases of palatal myoclonus. There are no randomized trials, comparison groups, or independent replications. Both participants were young adults, and reported tremor-frequency changes were measured after treatment.

Human and clinical evidence

Agha et al. reported a 26-year-old woman with 2.5-Hz palatal tremor treated with 940-nm laser at 8.7 J/cm² over 20 sessions. Frequency fell to 0.11 Hz after treatment and remained between 0.12 and 0.36 Hz during seven years of follow-up; swallowing and sleep reportedly improved. A second case involved a 28-year-old man with 3-Hz tremor after dental extraction. He received 980-nm treatment at 13.3 J/cm² over two months, and tremor frequency was reported as 0.3 Hz within 60 days with symptom and functional improvement (Agha et al. 2026). The sample of two and absence of a control group make these observations highly uncertain.

Animal evidence

No animal evidence was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo evidence was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The two cases used different wavelengths, fluences, schedules, and treatment durations. One report describes 20 sessions and extended follow-up, while the second used treatment over two months. These case-specific parameters do not define a reproducible standard or show which component of treatment might matter. Measurement methods and timing also need prospective standardization.

Interpretation

The cases provide a signal for further study, not a reliable estimate of benefit. The database assigns Denmark as the country, while the article lists a United Arab Emirates affiliation; this country discrepancy is retained as a source-record limitation.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for reducing palatal tremor frequency and related symptoms
Publications and records1 publication describing 2 cases.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Evidence is limited to a two-person case report without a control group. Both cases describe large reductions in tremor frequency and improved symptoms after laser treatment, but spontaneous change, measurement variability, and concurrent care cannot be excluded. A controlled series with blinded frequency measurement and functional outcomes is needed before efficacy or durability can be judged.
